newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Gold gains in Europe as U.S. missiles hit Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Gold gains in Europe as U.S. missiles hit Iraq.

text.p: Gold prices firmed by around 50 cents an ounce in early European trade on Tuesday on news that the U.S. had struck targets in southern Iraq.
But prices were stabilising and room to rise was limited unless the conflict widened, dealers said.
"We are seeing buying from the Far East because of the U.S. strikes in Iraq," one dealer at a major Swiss bank said, noting the price had advanced to around $387.50.
"If the conflict does not escalate, prices are not likely to gain much. But now we have to wait and see," he added.
In Hong Kong, gold edged up slightly minutes after the U.S. launched the missile strikes, gold traders said.
"People are a little bit nervous," said Anderson Cheung, chief dealer at Swiss Bank Corporation, but he added that no major moves were expected.
"People remember 1991," Cheung said, noting that the market's experience during the Gulf War -- when gold prices soared and then collapsed -- had tempered any extreme reaction.
"I don't see gold at $400 because of this," another dealer at a big Swiss bank said, noting several traders still remembered how they lost lots of money by going long in gold during the Gulf War.

"No one wants to be short and have to explain to management why you are short when the United States just attacked Iraq," he added. But he said many traders saw the assault in the context of the U.S. election campaign and were not overly concerned.
Traders said they were watching to see whether U.S. funds would pile into gold and trigger follow-on buying in Europe.
The U.S. military on Tuesday launched cruise missile strikes against air defence targets in Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi military attackes against the Kurds, the Pentagon said.
The news had little impact in other metals markets, although traders and analysts said they would watch for further developments.
On the London Metal Exchange, copper eased by around $31 to $1,995 ahead of an expected increase in stocks in its warehouses. Prices had raced sharply higher on Monday.
